vignette: Arthur stands by the office window, watching the rain streak the glass. He does not turn around when the receptionist buzzes him about the afternoon assembly. The sharp click of her finger on the intercom button triggers a sudden, tight contraction in his chest, and he finds himself counting the ceiling tiles instead of answering. Fourteen months pass since the night in the east parking lot, since the metal of the brick wall meets his shoulder, since the stranger's knuckles catch him under the jaw, since the threat that he will not leave walking. He recalls the smell of wet asphalt and diesel, the way his keys scatter across the pavement, and the absolute, paralyzing certainty that he will not make it to his car. He still drives past that intersection on his way home. He never turns into the lot. Instead, he loops three blocks out of his way, a detour he memorizes and defends with rigid insistence. When his wife, Elena, asks why he returns home thirty minutes early from the district budget meeting, he tells her the committee runs long. He does not tell her that the fluorescent hum of the conference room now feels like the streetlights from that night, that his hands tremble when he reaches for his coffee, that he has stopped sleeping through the night. The bed feels like a vulnerability. He lies awake, listening for the crunch of gravel on the driveway, and when a car backfires in the distance, his heart hammers against his ribs until his vision whites out. At the school, Arthur once commands the hallways with a calm, measured voice. Now, he walks quickly, keeps his back to the wall, and scans the perimeter of every room before he steps inside. He delegates the late-night grading reviews to his assistant principal. He no longer sits alone in his office after closing, though he used to cherish that quiet. The silence now feels like an ambush waiting to happen. When a parent raises their voice during a drop-off conference, Arthur's throat closes. He forces himself to breathe, but his thoughts spiral backward, replaying the moment he realizes he has misjudged a man who smiles right before the first strike. He tells himself he should have seen it. He tells himself he fails to protect the space he is paid to guard. Elena notices the distance. She tries to hold his hand during dinner, and he flinches, pulling away before he can stop it. He loves her, but the intimacy feels dangerous now, a sudden drop into unknown terrain. He stops talking about the assault unless she brings it up first. Then he speaks in fragments, careful to leave out the parts that make his stomach turn, the parts that make him feel like a child again. The school staff senses the change. They whisper about his new routines, his canceled field trips, the way he no longer attends the faculty lounge on Fridays. He misses the murmur of their voices, the shared exhaustion, the sense of belonging. Instead, he sits in his car in the staff lot, engine running, until the tension in his shoulders finally drops. In this room, Arthur sits on the edge of the chair, his knees pressed together, his gaze fixed on the rug. He speaks about the weight of his name on the building, the expectation of composure, the quiet terror of being ordinary when the world demands he remain unshakable. He does not ask for help. He simply places his hands flat on his thighs, feels the steady pressure of the fabric, and waits for the next question. The rain continues against the window. He breathes in, counts to four, and remains.
